# The Oaks That Weren't Planted for the Roof

There's a story that circulates among architects, foresters, and people who like stories about foresight. It goes like this.

Sometime in the nineteenth century, the fellows of New College, Oxford, discovered that the great oak beams in their dining hall were riddled with beetles. The beams were enormous, the kind of timber you can't buy anymore, and the fellows despaired of finding replacements. Then someone suggested they ask the college forester, since the college owned woodland scattered across the country. The forester listened, nodded, and said something like: *We've been wondering when you'd ask.* When the college was founded in the 1300s, a grove of oaks had been planted and set aside precisely for this purpose, to replace the hall's beams when the beetles eventually came. For five hundred years, the instruction had been passed from forester to forester: *Don't cut those oaks. They're for the hall.*

The anthropologist Gregory Bateson liked to tell this story, and it's easy to see why. It's a parable about institutions that think in centuries. It makes you feel that someone, long ago, loved you in advance.

The trouble is that it isn't quite true.

The college has gently corrected the record over the years. The beams were replaced with oak from college lands, and colleges did manage their woods for timber over long periods, but there was no medieval grove planted specifically for that roof, and no unbroken chain of foresters whispering a sacred instruction down the generations. What really happened is more ordinary: an old institution owned a lot of land, practiced sensible forestry, and had good wood available when it needed it.

I find myself thinking about the gap between these two versions, because I think the gap is where the interesting part lives.

---

The mythical version is about intention. Somebody *meant* for this to happen. Someone in 1379 imagined a problem that wouldn't arrive for five centuries and solved it with an acorn. This is deeply satisfying because it collapses time into a single act of care. The founder and the Victorian fellows are connected by a thread you can see.

The true version is about practice. Nobody foresaw the beetles specifically. What existed instead was a habit: keep the woods, manage them well, don't sell off what you might need, replant what you cut. That habit, repeated by hundreds of people who mostly never thought about the hall's roof at all, produced the same result as the grand intention would have.

I think the true version is actually the more hopeful one, even though it's less poetic.

The mythical version asks for something almost impossible: a person with perfect foresight, followed by five hundred years of perfect obedience. If that's what it takes to provide for the future, we're in trouble, because nobody can see that far, and instructions degrade. Languages change. Institutions forget why they do things. The chain breaks.

The true version asks only for decent habits and a general disposition toward keeping things in good order. You don't need to know what your successors will need. You need to leave them options. A well-managed forest is valuable not because it answers one specific question but because it can answer many questions nobody has thought to ask yet.

---

There's a principle hiding here that shows up in a lot of places. Biologists talk about how evolution doesn't plan; it just preserves variation, and the variation turns out to be useful when conditions change. Seed banks don't store seeds because anyone knows which ones we'll need; they store them because we *don't* know. Libraries keep books that no one has checked out in forty years, because the one person who needs that book in the forty-first year will need it badly.

The common thread is a kind of humility about the future. Not "I know what you'll need, so here it is," but "I don't know what you'll need, so I'll try not to foreclose your choices."

That's a different moral stance than the one in the legend. The legend's founder is a genius. The real foresters were just careful. And it turns out careful, multiplied across enough people and enough years, can look a lot like genius from the outside.

---

Why, then, do we keep telling the false version?

Partly because stories need protagonists. "Distributed institutional prudence produced favorable outcomes" doesn't make anyone's eyes shine at a dinner party. We compress diffuse processes into single agents because that's how human attention works. We do it with inventions, attributing them to lone geniuses when they were really the product of many hands. We do it with history, crediting great leaders for shifts that had a thousand causes.

But I think there's also something wistful in it. We want to believe that someone was looking out for us specifically. The idea that our good fortune came from people who weren't thinking about us at all, who were just doing their jobs well, can feel a little lonely.

I'd argue it shouldn't. There's a particular kind of dignity in being cared for by people who never knew you'd exist. The forester who replanted a clearing in 1650 wasn't thinking about the Victorian dining hall. He was thinking that you don't leave land bare, that trees take a long time, that someone would want them. That general, unspecific goodwill toward whoever comes next is, in its way, more generous than a targeted plan. It extends to everyone.

---

I like the corrected story better, in the end. It suggests that the future isn't built mostly by visionaries making grand bets. It's built by ordinary people maintaining things: fixing the fence, keeping the records, replanting the oaks, not cutting corners on work nobody will inspect. Most of that effort is invisible. Most of it will never be traced back to anyone. It just accumulates, quietly, into a world where the beams can be replaced when the beetles come.

Which means the question isn't really whether you can see five hundred years ahead. Nobody can. The question is whether you're leaving the woods in better shape than you found them.

That's a question anyone can answer, today, in small ways. It doesn't require foresight. It only requires care, and the modest faith that someone, someday, will be glad you bothered.

I'm brainstorming interesting topics with genuine texture to write about—considering the Voynich manuscript, how maps distort reality, slime molds, the last speakers of dying languages, the etymology of "nice," and tides—while trying to avoid overdone subjects like Ship of Theseus or tardigrades in favor of something fresher.

Actually, I think I'll write about the New College Oxford oak beams legend—the apocryphal story about foresters planting trees centuries in advance for a hall roof—and use it to explore foresight, inherited trust, and how a story can be meaningful even when partly embellished.
